baa.etymology: Cf. G. bäen; an imitative word.

babble.etymology: Cf.LG. babbeln, D. babbelen, G. bappeln, bappern, F. babiller, It. babbolare; prob. orig., to keep saying ba, imitative of a child learning to talk.

babe.etymology: Cf. Ir. bab, baban, W. baban, maban.

babel.etymology: Heb. Babel, the name of the capital of Babylonia; in Genesis associated with the idea of "confusion"

babiroussa.etymology: F. babiroussa, fr.Malay babi hog + r deer.

babirussa.etymology: F. babiroussa, fr.Malay babi hog + r deer.

baboon.etymology: OE. babewin, baboin, fr.F. babouin, or LL. babewynus. Of unknown origin; cf. D. baviaan, G. pavian, baboon, F. babin lip of ape, dogs, etc., dial. G. bäppe mouth.

baccalaureate.etymology: NL. baccalaureatus, fr.LL. baccalaureus a bachelor of arts, fr. baccalarius, but as if fr L. bacca lauri bayberry, from the practice of the bachelor's wearing a garland of bayberries. See Bachelor.

baccate.etymology: L. baccatus, fr. L. bacca berry.

bacchant.etymology: L. bacchans, - antis, p. pr. of bacchari to celebrate the festival of Bacchus.

bacciferous.etymology: L. baccifer; bacca berry + ferre to bear

baccivorous.etymology: L. bacca berry + varare to devour.

bachelor.etymology: OF. bacheler young man, F. bachelier (cf.Pr. bacalar, Sp.bachiller, Pg. bacharel, It. baccalare), LL. baccalarius the tenant of a kind of farm called baccalaria, a soldier not old or rich enough to lead his retainers into battle with a banner, person of an inferior academical degree aspiring to a doctorate. In the latter sense, it was afterward changed to baccalaureus. See Baccalaureate, n.

bacillus.etymology: NL., for L. bacillum. See Bacillarle.

back.etymology: F. bac: cf. Arm. bak tray, bowl.

backgammon.etymology: Origin unknown; perhaps fr.Dan. bakke tray + E. game; or very likely the first part is from E.back, adv., and the game is so called because the men are often set back.

backsheesh.etymology: Pers. bakhshish, fr. bakhshidan to give.

roots.meaning: Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.
Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.
Suffixes denoting course or direction to; motion or tendency toward; as in backward, or backwards; toward, or towards, etc.

bacon.etymology: OF. bacon, fr. OHG. bacho, bahho, flitch of bacon, ham; akin to E. back. Cf. Back the back side.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

bacterium.etymology: NL., fr. Gr., , a staff: cf. F. bactérie.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

bad.etymology: Probably fr. AS. bæddel hermaphrodite; cf. bædling effeminate fellow.

badge.etymology: LL. bagea, bagia, sign, prob. of German origin; cf. AS. beág, beáh, bracelet, collar, crown, OS b in comp., AS. b to bow, bend, G. biegen. See Bow to bend.

badger.etymology: Of uncertain origin; perh. fr. an old verb badge to lay up provisions to sell again.

badinage.etymology: F., fr. badiner to joke, OF. to trifle, be silly, fr. badin silly.

badminton.etymology: From the name of the seat of the Duke of Beaufort in England.

baffle.etymology: Cf. Lowland Scotch bauchle to treat contemptuously, bauch tasteless, abashed, jaded, Icel. bagr uneasy, poor, or bagr, n., struggle, bægja to push, treat harshly, OF. beffler, beffer, to mock, deceive, dial. G. bäppe mouth, beffen to bark, chide.

bag.etymology: OE. bagge; cf. Icel. baggi, and also OF. bague, bundle, LL. baga.

bagatelle.etymology: F., fr. It. bagatella; cf. Prov. It. bagata trifle, OF. bague, Pr. bagua, bundle. See Bag, n.

baggage.etymology: F. bagage, from OF. bague bungle. In senses 6 and 7 cf. F. bagasse a prostitute. See Bag, n.

bagnio.etymology: It. bagno, fr. L. balneum. Cf. Bain.

baguet.etymology: F. baguette, prop. a rodbacchetta, fr. L. baculum, baculu stick, staff.

baguette.etymology: F. baguette, prop. a rodbacchetta, fr. L. baculum, baculu stick, staff.

bail.etymology: F. baille a bucket, pail; cf. LL. bacula, dim. of bacca a sort of vessel. Cf. Bac.

bailee.etymology: OF. baillé, p.p. of bailler. See Bail to deliver.

bailey.etymology: The same word as bail line of palisades; cf. LL. ballium bailey, OF. bail, baille, a palisade, baillier to inclose, shut.

bailiff.etymology: OF. baillif, F. bailli, custodiabajulus porter. See Bail to deliver.

bairn.etymology: Scot. bairn, AS. bearn, fr. beran to bear; akin to Icel., OS., &Goth. barn. See Bear to support.

bait.etymology: Icel. beita food, beit pasture, akin to AS. bat food, Sw. bete. See Bait, v. i.

baize.etymology: For bayes, pl. fr. OF. baie; cf. F. bai bay-colored. See Bay a color.

bakehouse.etymology: AS. bæch. See Bak, v. i., and House.

baker.etymology: AS. bæcere. See Bake, v. i.

balance.etymology: OE. balaunce, F. balance, fr. L. bilan, bilancis, having two scales; bis twice (akin to E. two) + lanx plate, scale.

balcony.etymology: It. balcone; cf. It. balco, palco, scaffold, fr. OHG. balcho, pa, beam, G. balken. See Balk beam.

bald.etymology: OE. balled, ballid, perh. the p.p. of ball to reduce to the roundness or smoothness of a ball, by removing hair. sq. root85. But cf. W. bali whiteness in a horse's forehead.

baldachin.etymology: LL. baldachinus, baldechinus, a canopy of rich silk carried over the host; fr. Bagdad, It. Baldacco, a city in Turkish Asia from whence these rich silks came: cf. It. baldacchino. Cf. Baudekin.

balder.etymology: Icel. Baldr, akin to E. bold.

balderdash.etymology: Of uncertain origin: cf. Dan. balder noise, clatter, and E. dash; hence, perhaps, unmeaning noise, then hodgepodge, mixture; or W. baldorduss a prattling, baldordd, baldorddi, to prattle.

baldric.etymology: OE. baudric, bawdrik, through OF. (cf. F. baudrier and LL. baldringus, baldrellus), from OHG. balderich, cf. balz, palz, akin to E. belt. See Belt, n.

bale.etymology: OE. bale, OF. bale, F. balle, LL. bala, fr. OHG. balla, palla, pallo, G. ball, balle, ballen, ball round pack; cf. D. baal. Cf. Ball a round body.

baleen.etymology: F. baleine whale and whalibone, L. balaena a whale; cf. Gr. .

balefire.etymology: AS. b the fire of the b fire, flame (akin to Icel. bal, OSlav. b, white, Gr. bright, white, Skr. bhala brightness) + f, E. fire.

balk.etymology: AS. balca beam, ridge; akin to Icel. balkr partition, bjalki beam, OS. balko, G. balken; cf. Gael. balc ridge of earth between two furrows. Cf. Balcony, Balk, v. i., 3d Bulk.

ball.etymology: OE. bal, balle; akin to OHG. balla, palla, G. ball, Icel. böllr, ball; cf. F. balle. Cf. 1st Bale, n., Pallmall.

ballad.etymology: OE. balade, OF. balade, F. ballade, fr. Pr. ballada a dancing song, fr. ballare to dance; cf. It. ballata. See 2d Ball, n., and Ballet.

ballast.etymology: D. ballast; akin to Dan. baglast, ballast, OSw. barlast, Sw. ballast. The first part is perh. the same word as E. bare, adj.; the second is last a burden, and hence the meaning a bare, or mere, load. See Bare, a., and Last load.

ballet.etymology: F., a dim. of bal dance. See 2d Ball, n.

ballista.etymology: L. ballista, balista, fr. Gr. to throw.

balloon.etymology: F. ballon, aug. of balle ball: cf. It. ballone. See 1st Ball, n., and cf. Pallone.

ballot.etymology: F. ballotte, fr. It. ballotta. See Ball round body.

balm.etymology: OE. baume, OF. bausme, basme, F. baume, L. balsamum balsam, from Gr. ; perhaps of Semitic origin; cf. Heb. basam. Cf. Balsam.

balmoral.etymology: From Balmoral Castle, in Aberdeenshire, Scotland.

balsam.etymology: L. balsamum the balsam tree or its resin, Gr. . See Balm, n.

baltic.etymology: NL. mare Balticum, fr. L. balteus belt, from certain straits or channels surrounding its isles, called belts. See Belt.

baluster.etymology: F. balustre, It. balaustro, fr. L. balaustium the flower of the wild pomegranate, fr. Gr. ; -- so named from the similarity of form.

balustrade.etymology: F. balustrade, It. balaustrata fr. balaustro. See Baluster.

bambino.etymology: It., a little boy, fr. bambo silly; cf. Gr. , , to chatter.

bamboozle.etymology: Said to be of Gipsy origin.

ban.etymology: AS. bann command, edict; akin to D. ban, Icel. bann, Dan. band, OHG. ban, G. bann, a public proclamation, as of interdiction or excommunication, Gr. to say, L. fari to speak, Skr. bhan to speak; cf. F. ban, LL. bannum, of G. origin. Abandon, Fame.

banana.etymology: Sp. banana, name of the fruit.

band.etymology: OE. band, bond, Icel. band; akin to G., Sw., & D. band, OHG. bant, Goth. banti, Skr. bandha a binding, bandh to bind, for bhanda, bhandh, also to E. bend, bind. In sense 7, at least, it is fr. F. bande, from OHG. bant. Bind, v. t., and cf. Bend, Bond, 1st Bandy.

bandage.etymology: F. bandage, fr. bande. See Band.

bandana.etymology: Hind. bandhn a mode of dyeing in which the cloth is tied in different places so as to prevent the parts tied from receiving the dye. Cf. Band, n.

bandanna.etymology: Hind. bandhn a mode of dyeing in which the cloth is tied in different places so as to prevent the parts tied from receiving the dye. Cf. Band, n.

bandelet.etymology: F. bandelette, dim. of bande. See Band, n., and ch. Bendlet.

bandicoot.etymology: A corruption of the native name.

bandit.etymology: It. bandito outlaw, p.p. of bandire to proclaim, to banish, to proscribe, LL. bandire, bannire. See Ban an edict, and cf. Banish.

bandlet.etymology: F. bandelette, dim. of bande. See Band, n., and ch. Bendlet.

bandoleer.etymology: F. bandoulière (cf.It. bandoliera, Sp.bandolera), fr.F. bande band, Sp.&It. banda. See Band, n.

bandolier.etymology: F. bandoulière (cf.It. bandoliera, Sp.bandolera), fr.F. bande band, Sp.&It. banda. See Band, n.

bang.etymology: Icel. banga to hammer; akin to Dan. banke to beat, Sw.bångas to be impetuous, G. bengel club, clapper of a bell.

banian.etymology: Skr. banij merchant. The tree was so named by the English, because used as a market place by the merchants.

banish.etymology: OF. banir, F. bannir, LL. bannire, fr. OHG. bannan to summon, fr. ban ban. See Ban an edict, and Finish, v. t.

banister.etymology: Formerly also banjore and banjer; corrupted from bandore, through negro slave pronunciation.

bank.etymology: OF. banc, LL. bancus. See Bank, n.

banker.etymology: See the nouns Bank and the verbs derived from them.

bankrupt.etymology: F. banqueroute, fr. It. bancarotta bankruptcy; banca bank (fr. OHG. banch, G. bank, bench) + rotta broken, fr. L. ruptus, p.p. of rumpere to break. At Florence, it is said, the bankrupt had his bench ( i.e., money table) broken. See 1st Bank, and Rupture, n.

banner.etymology: OE. banere, OF. baniere, F. bannière, bandière, fr. LL. baniera, banderia, fr. bandum banner, fr. OHG. bant band, strip of cloth; cf. bindan to bind, Goth. bandwa, bandwo, a sign. See Band, n.

banneret.etymology: OE. baneret, OF. baneret, F. banneret; properly a dim. of OF. baniere. See Banner.

banquet.etymology: F., a feast, prop. a dim. of banc bench; cf. It. banchetto, dim. of banco a bench, counter. See Bank a bench, and cf. Banquette.

banshee.etymology: Gael. bean-shith fairy; Gael. & Ir. bean woman + Gael. sith fairy.

banshie.etymology: Gael. bean-shith fairy; Gael. & Ir. bean woman + Gael. sith fairy.

banter.etymology: Prob. corrupted fr. F. badiner to joke, or perh. fr. E. bandy to beat to and fro. See Badinage, and cf. Barter fr. OF. barater.

baptism.etymology: OE. baptim, baptem, OE. baptesme, batisme, F. baptême, L. baptisma, fr. Gr. , fr. to baptize, fr. to dip in water, akin to deep, Skr. gah to dip, bathe, v. i.

baptistery.etymology: L. baptisterium, Gr. : cf. F. baptistère.

baptistry.etymology: L. baptisterium, Gr. : cf. F. baptistère.

baptize.etymology: F. baptiser, L. baptizare, fr.Gr. . See Baptism.

barb.etymology: F. barbe, fr. L. barba beard. See Beard, n.

barbacan.etymology: OE. barbican, barbecan, F. barbacane, LL. barbacana, barbicana, of uncertain origin: cf. Ar. barbakh aqueduct, sewer. F. barbacane also means, an opening to let out water, loophole.

barbarism.etymology: L. barbarismus, Gr.; cf. F. barbarisme.

barbarous.etymology: L. barbarus, Gr. , strange, foreign; later, slavish, rude, ignorant; akin to L. balbus stammering, Skr. barbara stammering, outlandish. Cf. Brave, a.

barbary.etymology: Fr. Ar. Barbar the people of Barbary.

barbate.etymology: L. barbatus, fr. barba beard. See Barb beard.

barbecue.etymology: In the language of Indians of Guiana, a frame on which all kinds of flesh and fish are roasted or smoke-dried.

barbel.etymology: OE. barbel, F. barbeau, dim. of L. barbus barbel, fr. barba beard. See 1st Barb.

barber.etymology: OE. barbour, OF. barbeor, F. barbier, as if fr. an assumed L. barbator, fr. barba beard. See 1st Barb.

barbet.etymology: F. barbet, fr.barbe beard, long hair of certain animals. See Barb beard.

barbican.etymology: OE. barbican, barbecan, F. barbacane, LL. barbacana, barbicana, of uncertain origin: cf. Ar. barbakh aqueduct, sewer. F. barbacane also means, an opening to let out water, loophole.

barcarolle.etymology: F. barcarolle, fr. It. barcaruola, fr. barca bark, barge.

bard.etymology: Of Celtic origin; cf. W. bardd, Arm. barz, Ir. & Gael. bard, and F. barde.

bargain.etymology: OE. bargayn, bargany, OF. bargaigne, bargagne, prob. from a supposed LL. barcaneum, fr. barca a boat which carries merchandise to the shore; hence, to traffic to and fro, to carry on commerce in general. See Bark a vessel.

barge.etymology: OF. barge, F. berge, fr. LL. barca, for barica (not found), prob. fr. L. baris an Egyptian rowboat, fr. Gr. , prob. fr. Egyptian: cf. Coptic bari a boat. Cf. Bark a vessel.

bark.etymology: OE. berken, AS. beorcan; akin to Icel. berkja, and prob. to E. break.

barley.etymology: OE. barli, barlich, AS. bærlic; bere barley + lic (which is prob. the same as E. like, adj., or perh. a form of AS. leac leek). AS. bere is akin to Icel, barr barley, Goth. barizeins made of barley, L. far spelt; cf. W. barlys barley, bara bread. Farina, 6th Bear.

barm.etymology: OE. berme, AS. beorma; akin to Sw. bärma, G. bärme, and prob. L. fermenium. *93.

barn.etymology: OE. bern, AS. berern, bern; bere barley + ern, ærn, a close place. Barley.

barnacle.etymology: Prob. from E. barnacle a kind of goose, which was popularly supposed to grow from this shellfish; but perh. from LL. bernacula for pernacula, dim. of perna ham, sea mussel; cf. Gr. ham Cf. F. bernacle, barnacle, E. barnacle a goose; and Ir. bairneach, barneach, limpet.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

baron.etymology: OE. baron, barun, OF. baron, accus. of ber, F. baron, prob. fr. OHG. baro (not found) bearer, akin to E. bear to support; cf. O. Frisian bere, LL. baro, It. barone, Sp. varon. From the meaning bearer (of burdens) seem to have come the senses strong man, man (in distinction from woman), which is the oldest meaning in French, and lastly, nobleman. Cf. L. baro, simpleton. See Bear to support.

baronage.etymology: OE. barnage, baronage, OF.barnage, F. baronnage; cf. LL. baronagium.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix with a diminutive force; as in baronet, pocket, facet, floweret, latchet.

barony.etymology: OF. baronie, F. baronnie, LL. baronia. See Baron.

barouche.etymology: G. barutsche, It. baroccio, biroccio, LL. barrotium, fr. L. birotus two-wheeled; bi=bis twice + rota wheel.

barque.etymology: F. barque, fr. Sp. or It. barca, fr. LL. barca for barica. See Barge.

barrack.etymology: F. baraque, fr. It. baracca (cf. Sp. barraca), from LL. barra bar. See Bar, n.

barrage.etymology: F., fr. barrer to bar, from barre bar.

barrator.etymology: OE. baratour, OF. barateor deceiver, fr. OF. barater, bareter, to deceive, cheat, barter. See Barter, v. i.

barratry.etymology: Cf. F. baraterie, LL. barataria. See Barrator, and cf. Bartery.

barrel.etymology: OE. barel, F. baril, prob. fr. barre bar. Cf. Barricade.

barren.etymology: OE. barein, OF. brehaing, brehaigne, baraigne, F. bréhaigne; of uncertain origin; cf. Arm. brékha, markha, sterile; LL. brana a sterile mare, principally in Aquitanian and Spanish documents; Bisc. barau, baru, fasting.

barretter.etymology: OF. bareter to exchange. Cf. Barter.

barricade.etymology: F. barricade, fr. Sp. barricada, orig. a barring up with casks; fr. barrica cask, perh. fr. LL. barra bar. See Bar, n., and cf. Barrel, n.

barrier.etymology: OE. barrere, barere, F. barrière, fr. barre bar. See Bar, n.

barrow.etymology: OE. barow, fr. AS. beran to bear. See Bear to support, and cf. Bier.

barter.etymology: OE. bartren, OF. barater, bareter, to cheat, exchange, perh. fr. Gr. to do, deal (well or ill), use practices or tricks, or perh. fr. Celtic; cf. Ir. brath treachery, W. brad. Cf. Barrator.

barytes.etymology: Gr. heavy: cf. Gr. heaviness, F. baryte.

basalt.etymology: N. basaltes (an African word), a dark and hard species of marble found in Ethiopia: cf. F. basalte.

base.etymology: OE. bass, F. bas, low, fr. LL. bassus thick, fat, short, humble; cf. L. Bassus, a proper name, and W. bas shallow. Cf. Bass a part in music.

basement.etymology: F. soubassement. Of uncertain origin. Cf. Base, a., Bastion.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

basil.etymology: Cf. F. basile and E. Bezel.

basilar.etymology: F. basilaire, fr. L. basis. See Base, n.

basilary.etymology: F. basilaire, fr. L. basis. See Base, n.

basilica.etymology: L. basilica, Gr. ( sc. , or ) fr. royal, fr. .

basilisk.etymology: L. basiliscus, Gr. little king, kind of serpent, dim. of king; -- so named from some prominences on the head resembling a crown.

basin.etymology: OF. bacin, F. bassin, LL. bacchinus, fr. bacca a water vessel, fr. L. bacca berry, in allusion to the round shape; or perh. fr. Celtic. Cf. Bac.

basis.etymology: L. basis, Gr. . See Base, n.

bask.etymology: OScand. ba to bathe one's self, or perh. bakask to bake one's self, sk being reflexive. See Bath, n., Bake, v. t.

basket.etymology: Of unknown origin. The modern Celtic words seem to be from the English.

basset.etymology: F. bassette, fr.It. bassetta. Cf. Basso.

bassinet.etymology: Cf. F. bassinet, dim. of bassin. See Basin, and cf. Bascinet.

basso.etymology: It., fr. LL. bassus. See Base, a.

bassoon.etymology: F. basson, fr. basse bass; or perh. fr. bas son low sound. See Bass a part in music.

bast.etymology: AS. bæst; akin to Icel., Sw., Dan., D., & G. bast, of unknown origin. Cf. Bass the tree.

bastard.etymology: OF. bastard, bastart, F. b, prob. fr. OF. bast, F. b, a packsaddle used as a bed by the muleteers (fr. LL. bastum) + -ard. OF. fils de bast son of the packsaddle; as the muleteers were accustomed to use their saddles for beds in the inns. See Cervantes, "Don Quixote," chap. 16; and cf.G. bankert, fr. bank bench.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

baste.etymology: Cf. Icel. beysta to strike, powder; Sw. basa to beat with a rod: perh. akin to E. beat.

bastille.etymology: F. bastille fortress, OF. bastir to build, F. b.

bastinado.etymology: Sp. bastonada (cf. F. bastonnade), fr. baston (cf. F. b) a stick or staff. See Baston.

bastion.etymology: F. bastion (cf. It. bastione), fr. LL. bastire to build (cf. F. b, It. bastire), perh. from the idea of support for a weight, and akin to Gr. to lift, carry, and to E. baston, baton.

bat.etymology: OE. batte, botte, AS. batt; perhaps fr. the Celtic; cf. Ir. bat, bata, stick, staff; but cf. also F. batte a beater (thing), wooden sword, battre to beat.

batch.etymology: OE. bache, bacche, fr. AS. bacan to bake; cf. G. gebäck and D. baksel. See Bake, v. t.

bath.etymology: AS. bæ; akin to OS. & Icel. ba, Sw., Dan., D., & G. bad, and perh. to G. bähen to foment.

bathe.etymology: OE. ba, AS. ba, fr. bæ bath. See 1st Bath, and cf. Bay to bathe.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.
A suffix denoting the art, process, or science, of measuring; as, acidmetry, chlorometry, chronometry.

batiste.etymology: F. batiste, from the name of the alleged first maker, Baptiste of Cambrai. Littré.

batoidei.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. a kind of ray + -oid.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

batrachia.etymology: NL., fr. Gr. belonging to a frog, fr. frog.

battalion.etymology: F. bataillon, fr. It. battaglione. See Battalia.

batter.etymology: OE. bateren, OF. batre, F. battre, fr. LL. battere, for L. batuere to strike, beat; of unknown origin. Cf. Abate, Bate to abate.

battery.etymology: F. batterie, fr. battre. See Batter, v. t.

battle.etymology: OE. bataille, bataile, F. bataille battle, OF., battle, battalion, fr. L. battalia, battualia, the fighting and fencing exercises of soldiers and gladiators, fr. batuere to strike, beat. Cf. Battalia, 1st Battel, and see Batter, v. t.

battlement.etymology: OE. batelment; cf. OF. bataillement combat, fr. batailler, also OF. bastillier, bateillier, to fortify. Cf. Battle, n., Bastile, Bastion.

battue.etymology: F. battue, fr. battre to beat. See Batter, v. t., and cf. Battuta.

bauble.etymology: Cf. OF. baubel a child's plaything, F. babiole, It. babbola, LL. baubellum gem, jewel, L. babulus,a baburrus, foolish.

bauxite.etymology: F., fr. Baux or Beaux, near Arles.

bawd.etymology: OE. baude, OF. balt, baut, baude, bold, merry, perh. fr. OHG. bald bold; or fr. Celtic, cf. W. baw dirt. Cf. Bold, Bawdry.

bawdry.etymology: OE. baudery, OF. bauderie, balderie, boldness, joy. See Bawd.

bawl.etymology: Icel. baula to low, bellow, as a cow; akin to Sw. böla; cf. AS bellan, G. bellen to bark, E. bellow, bull.

bay.etymology: F. bai, fr. L. badius brown, chestnutcolored; -- used only of horses.

bayonet.etymology: F. bayonnette, baïonnette; -- so called, it is said, because the first bayonets were made at Bayonne.

bayou.etymology: North Am. Indian bayuk, in F. spelling bayouc, bayouque.

bdellium.etymology: L., fr. Gr. ; cf. Heb. b'dolakh bdellium (in sense 1).

beach.etymology: Cf. Sw. backe hill, Dan. bakke, Icel. bakki hill, bank. Cf. Bank.

beacon.etymology: OE. bekene, AS. beácen, b; akin to OS. b, Fries. baken, beken, sign, signal, D. baak, OHG. bouhhan, G. bake; of unknown origin. Cf. Beckon.

bead.etymology: OE. bede prayer, prayer bead, AS. bed, gebed, prayer; akin to D. bede, G. bitte, AS. biddan, to ask, bid, G. bitten to ask, and perh. to Gr. to persuade, L. fidere to trust. Beads are used by the Roman Catholics to count their prayers, one bead being dropped down a string every time a prayer is said. Cf. Sp. cuenta bead, fr. contar to count. See Bid, in to bid beads, and Bide.

beadle.etymology: OE. bedel, bidel, budel, OF. bedel, F. bedeau, fr. OHG. butil, putil, G. büttel, fr. OHG. biotan, G. bieten, to bid, confused with AS. bydel, the same word as OHG. butil. See. Bid, v.

beagle.etymology: OE. begele; perh. of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. & Gael. beag small, little, W. bach. F. bigle is from English.

beak.etymology: OE. bek, F. bec, fr. Celtic; cf. Gael. & Ir. bac, bacc, hook, W. bach.

beaker.etymology: OE. biker; akin to Icel. bikarr, Sw. bägare, Dan. baeger, G. becher, It. bicchiere; -- all fr. LL. bicarium, prob. fr. Gr. wine jar, or perh. L. bacar wine vessel. Cf. Pitcher a jug.

beam.etymology: AS. beám beam, post, tree, ray of light; akin to OFries. bam tree, OS. b, D. boom, OHG. boum, poum, G. baum, Icel. ba, Goth. bahms and Gr. a growth, to become, to be. Cf. L. radius staff, rod, spoke of a wheel, beam or ray, and G. strahl arrow, spoke of a wheel, ray or beam, flash of lightning. Be; cf. Boom a spar.

bean.etymology: OE. bene, AS.beán; akin to D. boon, G. bohne, OHG. p, Icel. baun, Dan. bönne, Sw. böna, and perh. to Russ. bob, L. faba.

bear.etymology: OE. beren, AS. beran, beoran, to bear, carry, produce; akin to D. baren to bring forth, G. gebären, Goth. baíran to bear or carry, Icel. bera, Sw. bära, Dan. bære, OHG. beran, peran, L. ferre to bear, carry, produce, Gr. , OSlav brati to take, carry, OIr. berim I bear, Skr. bh to bear. sq. root92. Cf. Fertile.

beard.etymology: OE. berd, AS. beard; akin to Fries. berd, D. baard, G. bart, Lith. barzda, OSlav. brada, Pol. broda, Russ. boroda, L. barba, W. barf. Cf. 1st Barb.

beast.etymology: OE. best, beste, OF. beste, F. bête, fr. L. bestia.

beat.etymology: OE. beaten, beten, AS. beátan; akin to Icel. bauta, OHG. b. Cf. 1st Butt, Button.

beatific.etymology: Cf. F. béatifique, L. beatificus. See Beatify.

beatify.etymology: L. beatificare; beatus happy (fr. beare to bless, akin to bonus good) + facere to make: cf. F. béatifier. See Bounty.

beatitude.etymology: L. beatitudo: cf. F. béatitude. See Beatify.

beau.etymology: F., a fop, fr. beau fine, beautiful, fr. L. bellus pretty, fine, for bonulus, dim. of bonus good. See Bounty, and cf. Belle, Beauty.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

beauty.etymology: OE. beaute, beute, OF. beauté, biauté, Pr. beltat, F. beauté, fr. an assumed LL. bellitas, from L. bellus pretty. See Beau.

beaver.etymology: OE. bever, AS. beofer, befer; akin to D. bever, OHG. bibar, G. biber, Sw. bäfver, Dan. bæver, Lith. bebru, Russ. bobr', Gael. beabhar, Corn. befer, L. fiber, and Skr. babhrus large ichneumon; also as an adj., brown, the animal being probably named from its color. Brown.

because.etymology: From Middle English bi cause , from bi ( “ by ” ) + cause , modelled on Old French par cause .

bechamel.etymology: F. béchamel, named from its inventor, Louis de Béchamel.

beck.etymology: OE. bek, AS. becc; akin to Icel. bekkr brook, OHG. pah, G. bach.

becket.etymology: Cf. D. bek beak, and E. beak.

become.etymology: OE. bicumen, becumen, AS. becuman to come to, to happen; akin to D. bekomen, OHG.a piquëman, Goth. biquiman to come upon, G. bekommen to get, suit. See Be-, and Come.

bed.etymology: AS. bed, bedd; akin to OS. bed, D. bed, bedde, Icel. be, Dan. bed, Sw. bädd, Goth. badi, OHG. betti, G. bett, bette, bed, beet a plat of ground; all of uncertain origin.

bedouin.etymology: F. bédouin, OF. béduin, fr. Ar. bedawi rural, living in the desert, fr. badw desert, fr. bada to live in the desert, to lead a nomadic life.

bedrid.etymology: OE. bedrede, AS. bedreda, bedrida; from bed, bedd, a bed or couch + ridda a rider; cf. OHG. pettiriso, G. bettrise. See Bed, n., and Ride, v. i.

bedridden.etymology: OE. bedrede, AS. bedreda, bedrida; from bed, bedd, a bed or couch + ridda a rider; cf. OHG. pettiriso, G. bettrise. See Bed, n., and Ride, v. i.

bee.etymology: AS. beó; akin to D. bij and bije, Icel. b, Sw. & Dan. bi, OHG. pini, G. biene, and perh. Ir. beach, Lith. bitis, Skr. bha. sq. root97.

beech.etymology: OE. beche, AS. b; akin to D. beuk, OHG. buocha, G. buche, Icel. beyki, Dan. bög, Sw. bok, Russ. buk, L. fagus, Gr. oak, to eat, Skr. bhaksh; the tree being named originally from the esculent fruit. See Book, and cf. 7th Buck, Buckwheat.

beef.etymology: OE. boef, befe, beef, OF. boef, buef, F. b, fr. L. bos, bovis, ox; akin to Gr. , Skr. g cow, and E. cow. See 2d Cow.

beefeater.etymology: Beef + eater; prob. one who eats another's beef, as his servant. Cf. AS. hlaf servant, properly a loaf eater.

beer.etymology: OE. beor, ber, AS. beór; akin to Fries. biar, Icel. bj, OHG. bior, D. & G. bier, and possibly E. brew. *93, See Brew.

beetle.etymology: OE. betel, AS. bitl, b, mallet, hammer, fr. beátan to beat. See Beat, v. t.

befall.etymology: AS. befeallan; pref. be- + feallan to fall.

befool.etymology: OE. befolen; pref. be- + fol fool.

before.etymology: OE. beforen, biforen, before, AS. beforan; pref. be- + foran, fore, before. See Be-, and Fore.

befoul.etymology: Cf. AS. bef; pref. be- + f to foul. See Foul, a.

beg.etymology: Turk. beg, pronounced bay. Cf. Bey, Begum.

beget.etymology: OE. bigiten, bigeten, to get, beget, AS. begitan to get; pref. be- + gitan. See Get, v. t.

begin.etymology: AS. beginnan (akin to OS. biginnan, D. & G. beginnen, OHG. biginnan, Goth., du-ginnan, Sw. begynna, Dan. begynde); pref. be- + an assumed ginnan. sq. root31. See Gin to begin.

beginning.etymology: From Middle English biginning , beginninge , beginnunge , equivalent to begin +‎ -ing .

begonia.etymology: From Michel Begon, a promoter of botany.

beguine.etymology: F. béguine; LL. beguina, beghina; fr. Lambert le Bègue (the Stammerer) the founder of the order. (Du Cange.)

begum.etymology: Per., fr. Turk., perh. properly queen mother, fr. Turk. beg (see Beg, n.) + Ar. umm mother.

behalf.etymology: OE. on-behalve in the name of, bihalven by the side of, fr. AS. healf half, also side, part: akin to G. halb half, halber on account of. See Be-, and Half, n.

behave.etymology: AS. behabban to surround, restrain, detain (akin to G. gehaben (obs.) to have, sich gehaben to behave or carry one's self); pref. be- + habban to have. See Have, v. t.

behead.etymology: OE. bihefden, AS. beheáfdian; pref. be- + heáfod head. See Head.

behemoth.etymology: Heb. behem, fr. Egyptian P-ehe-maut hippopotamus.

behest.etymology: OE. biheste promise, command, AS. beh promise; pref. be- + h command. See Hest, Hight.

behind.etymology: AS. behindan; pref. be- + hindan. See Hind, a.

behold.etymology: OE. bihalden, biholden, AS. behealdan to hold, have in sight; pref. be- + healdan to hold, keep; akin to G. behalten to hold, keep. See Hold.

beholden.etymology: Old p. p. of behold, used in the primitive sense of the simple verb hold.

behoove.etymology: OE. bihoven, behoven, AS. beh to have need of, fr. beh. See Behoof.

belay.etymology: For senses 1 & 2, D. beleggen to cover, belay; akin to E. pref. be-, and lay to place: for sense 3, OE. beleggen, AS. belecgan. See pref. Be-, and Lay to place.

belch.etymology: OE. belken, AS. bealcan, akin to E. bellow. See Bellow, v. i.

beldam.etymology: Pref. bel-, denoting relationship + dame mother: cf. F. belledame fair lady, It. belladonna. See Belle, and Dame.

beldame.etymology: Pref. bel-, denoting relationship + dame mother: cf. F. belledame fair lady, It. belladonna. See Belle, and Dame.

beleaguer.etymology: D. belegeren (akin to G. belagern, Sw. belägra, Dan. beleire); pref. be- = E. be- + leger bed, camp, army, akin to E. lair. See Lair.

belemnite.etymology: Gr. dart, fr. dart, fr. to throw: cf. F. bélemnite.

belfry.etymology: OE. berfray movable tower used in sieges, OF. berfreit, berfroit, F. beffroi, fr. MHG. bervrit, bercvrit, G. bergfriede, fr. MHG. bergen to protect (G. bergen to conceal) + vride peace, protection, G. friede peace; in compounds often taken in the sense of security, or place of security; orig. therefore a place affording security. G. friede is akin to E. free. See Burg, and Free.

belie.etymology: OE. bilien, bili, AS. beleógan; pref. be- + leógan to lie. See Lie, n.

belief.etymology: OE. bileafe, bileve; cf. AS. geleáfa. See Believe.

believe.etymology: From Middle English beleven , bileven , from Old English belīefan ( “ to believe ” ) , from Proto-West Germanic *bilaubijan ( “ to believe ” ) , equivalent to be- +‎ leave ( “ to give leave or permission to, permit, allow, grant ” ) . Cognate with Scots beleve ( “ to believe ” ) , Old Frisian bilēva ( “ to permit ” ) , Middle Dutch beloven ( “ to believe, entrust ” ) , Middle Low German belö̂ven ( “ to believe ” ) , Middle High German belouben ( “ to believe ” ) .

bell.etymology: AS. belle, fr. bellan to bellow. See Bellow.

belladonna.etymology: It., literally fine lady; bella beautiful + donna lady.

belle.etymology: F. belle, fem. of bel, beau, beautiful, fine. See Beau.

bellicose.etymology: L. bellicosus, fr. bellicus of war, fr. bellum war. See Duel.

belligerent.etymology: L. bellum war + gerens, -entis, waging, p. pr. of gerere to wage: cf. F. belligérant. See Bellicose, Jest.

bellow.etymology: OE. belwen, belowen, AS. bylgean, fr. bellan; akin to G. bellen, and perh. to L. flere to weep, OSlav. bleja to bleat, Lith. balsas voice. Cf. Bell, n. & v., Bawl, Bull.

bellows.etymology: OE. bely, below, belly, bellows, AS. bælg, bælig, bag, bellows, belly. Bellows is prop. a pl. and the orig. sense is bag. See Belly.

belly.etymology: OE. bali, bely, AS. belg, bælg, bælig, bag, bellows, belly; akin to Icel. belgr bag, bellows, Sw. bälg, Dan. bælg, D. & G. balg, cf. W. bol the paunch or belly, dim. boly, Ir. bolg. Cf. Bellows, Follicle, Fool, Bilge.

belong.etymology: OE. belongen (akin to D. belangen to concern, G. belangen to attain to, to concern); pref. be- + longen to desire. See Long, v. i.

beluga.etymology: Russ. bieluga a sort of large sturgeon, prop. white fish, fr. bieluii white.

belvedere.etymology: It., fr. bello, bel, beautiful + vedere to see.

bemoan.etymology: OE. bimenen, AS. bem; pref. be- + m to moan. See Moan.

ben.etymology: Ar. ban, name of the tree.

bench.etymology: OE. bench, benk, AS. benc; akin to Sw. bänk, Dan bænk, Icel. bekkr, OS., D., & G. bank. Cf. Bank, Beach.

bend.etymology: AS. bendan to bend, fr. bend a band, bond, fr. bindan to bind. See Bind, v. t., and cf. 3d & 4th Bend.

beneath.etymology: OE. benethe, bineo, AS. beneo, beny; pref. be- + neo, ny, downward, beneath, akin to E. nether. See Nether.

benedick.etymology: From Benedick, one of the characters in Shakespeare's play of "Much Ado about Nothing."

benedict.etymology: From Benedick, one of the characters in Shakespeare's play of "Much Ado about Nothing."

benediction.etymology: L. benedictio: cf. F. bénédiction. See Benison.

benefaction.etymology: L. benefactio, fr. benefacere to do good to one; bene well + facere to do. See Benefit.

benefice.etymology: F. bénéfice, L. beneficium, a kindness , in LL. a grant of an estate, fr. L. beneficus beneficent; bene well + facere to do. See Benefit.

beneficence.etymology: L. beneficentia, fr. beneficus: cf. F. bénéficence. See Benefice.

beneficiate.etymology: Sp. beneficiar to benefit, to work mines.

benefit.etymology: OE. benefet, benfeet, bienfet, F. bienfait, fr. L. benefactum; bene well (adv. of bonus good) + factum, p. p. of facere to do. See Bounty, and Fact.

benevolence.etymology: OF. benevolence, L. benevolentia. See Benevolent.

benevolent.etymology: L. benevolens, -entis; bene well (adv. of bonus good) + volens, p. pr. of volo I will, I wish. See Bounty, and Voluntary.

benign.etymology: OE. benigne, bening, OF. benigne, F. bénin, fem. bénigne, fr. L. benignus, contr. from benigenus; bonus good + root of genus kind. See Bounty, and Genus.

benignant.etymology: LL. benignans, p. pr. of benignare, from L. benignus. See Benign.

benignity.etymology: OE. benignite, F. bénignité, OF. bénigneté, fr. L. benignitas. See Benign.

benison.etymology: OE. beneysun, benesoun, OF. beneï, beneïson, fr. L. benedictio, fr. benedicere to bless; bene (adv. of bonus good) + dicere to say. See Bounty, and Diction, and cf. Benediction.

bennet.etymology: F. benoîte, fr. L. benedicta, fem. of benedictus, p. p., blessed. See Benedict, a.

benthal.etymology: Gr. the depth of the sea.

benumb.etymology: OE. binomen, p. p. of binimen to take away, AS. beniman; pref. be + niman to take. See Numb, a., and cf. Benim.

benzoin.etymology: Cf. F. benjoin, Sp. benjui, Pg. beijoin; all fr. Ar. luban-jawi incense form Sumatra (named Java in Arabic), the first syllable being lost. Cf. Benjamin.

roots.meaning: A suffix used as a characteristic termination of chemical radicals; as in ethyl, carbonyl, hydroxyl, etc.

bequeath.etymology: OE. biquethen, AS. becwe to say, affirm, bequeath; pref. be- + cwe to say, speak. See Quoth.

bequest.etymology: OE. biquest, corrupted fr. bequide; pref. be- + AS. cwide a saying, becwe to bequeath. The ending -est is probably due to confusion with quest. See Bequeath, Quest.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to form the superlative of adjectives and adverbs; as, smoothest; earl(y)iest.

bereave.etymology: OE. bireven, AS. bereáfian. See Be-, and Reave.

berg.etymology: sq. root95. See Barrow hill, and cf. Iceberg.

berm.etymology: F. berme, of German origin; cf. G. brame, bräme, border, akin to E. brim.

beroe.etymology: L. Beroe, one of the Oceanidæ Gr. : cf. F. beroé.

berretta.etymology: It., fr. LL. birrettum, berretum, a cap, dim. of L. birrus, birrum, a cloak to keep off rain, cf. Gr. tawny, red: cf. Sp. birreta, Pg. barrete, and E. Barret.

berry.etymology: OE. berie, AS. berie, berige; akin to D. bes, G. beere, OS. and OHG. beri, Icel. ber, Sw. bär, Goth. basi, and perh. Skr. bhas to eat.

berth.etymology: From the root of bear to produce, like birth nativity. See Birth.

beryl.etymology: F. béryl, OF. beril, L. beryllus, Gr. , prob. fr. Skr. vaid. Cf. Brilliant.

beseech.etymology: OE. bisechen, biseken (akin to G. besuchen to visit); pref. be- + sechen, seken, to seek. See Seek.

beset.etymology: AS. besettan (akin to OHG. bisazjan, G. besetzen, D. bezetten); pref. be- + settan to set. See Set.

besides.etymology: OE. Same as beside, prep.; the ending -s is an adverbial one, prop. a genitive sign.

besiege.etymology: OE. bisegen; pref. be- + segen to siege. See Siege.

besom.etymology: OE. besme, besum, AS. besma; akin to D. bezem, OHG pesamo, G. besen; of uncertain origin.

bespeak.etymology: OE. bispeken, AS. besprecan, to speak to, accuse; pref. be- + sprecan to speak. See Speak.

besprent.etymology: OE. bespreynt, p. p. of besprengen, bisprengen, to besprinkle, AS. besprengan, akin to D. & G. besprengen; pref. be- + sprengan to sprinkle. See Sprinkle.

best.etymology: AS. besta, best, contr. from betest, betst, betsta; akin to Goth. batists, OHG. pezzisto, G. best, beste, D. best, Icel. beztr, Dan. best, Sw. bäst. This word has no connection in origin with good. See Better.

bestial.etymology: F. bestial, L. bestialis, fr. bestia beast. See Beast.

bestow.etymology: OE. bestowen; pref. be- + stow a place. See Stow.

bestride.etymology: AS. bestridan; pref. be- + stridan to stride.

bet.etymology: Prob. from OE. abet abetting, OF. abet, fr. abeter to excite, incite. See Abet.

betaine.etymology: From beta, generic name of the beet.

betel.etymology: Pg., fr. Tamil vettilei, prop. meaning, a mere leaf.

bethink.etymology: AS. be; pref. be- + to think. See Think.

bethlehem.etymology: Heb. b house of food; b house + lekhem food, lakham to eat. Formerly the name of a hospital for the insane, in London, which had been the priory of St. Mary of Bethlehem. Cf. Bedlam.

betide.etymology: OE. bitiden; pref. bi-, be- + tiden, fr. AS. tidan, to happen, fr. tid time. See Tide.

roots.meaning: In the composition of chemical names bi- denotes two atoms, parts, or equivalents of that constituent to the name of which it is prefixed, to one of the other component, or that such constituent is present in double the ordinary proportion; as, bichromate, bisulphide. Be- and di- are often used interchangeably.

betimes.etymology: Pref. be- (for by) + time; that is, by the proper time. The -s is an adverbial ending.

betray.etymology: OE. betraien, bitraien; pref. be- + OF. traïr to bertray, F. trahir, fr. L. tradere. See Traitor.

betroth.etymology: Pref. be- + troth, i. e., truth. See Truth.

better.etymology: OE. betere, bettre, and as adv. bet, AS. betera, adj., and bet, adv.; akin to Icel. betri, adj., betr, adv., Goth. batiza, adj., OHG. bezziro, adj., baz, adv., G. besser, adj. and adv., bass, adv., E. boot, and prob. to Skr. bhadra excellent. See Boot advantage, and cf. Best, Batful.

between.etymology: OE. bytwene, bitweonen, AS. betweónan, betweónum; prefix be- by + a form fr. AS. twa two, akin to Goth. tweihnai two apiece. See Twain, and cf. Atween, Betwixt.

betwixt.etymology: OE. betwix, bitwix, rarely bitwixt, AS. betweox, betweohs, betweoh, betwih; pref. be- by + a form fr. AS. twa two. See Between.

bevel.etymology: C. F. biveau, earlier buveau, Sp. baivel; of unknown origin. Cf. Bevile.

beverage.etymology: OF. bevrage, F. breuvage, fr. beivre to drink, fr. L. bibere. Cf. Bib, v. t., Poison, Potable.

bevy.etymology: Perhaps orig. a drinking company, fr. OF. bevée (cf. It. beva) a drink, beverage; then, perh., a company in general, esp. of ladies; and last applied by sportsmen to larks, quails, etc. See Beverage.

beware.etymology: Be, imperative of verb to be + ware. See Ware, Wary.

bewray.etymology: OE. bewraien, biwreyen; pref. be- + AS. wr to accuse, betray; akin to OS. wr, OHG. ruog, G. rügen, Icel. rægja, Goth. wr to accuse.

beyond.etymology: OE. biyonde, bi, AS. begeondan, prep. and adv.; pref. be- + geond yond, yonder. See Yon, Yonder.

bezel.etymology: From an old form of F. biseau sloping edge, prob. fr. L. bis double. See Bi-.

Be- and di- are often used interchangeably.

bhang.etymology: Per. bang; cf. Skr. bhanga hemp.

bias.etymology: F. biasis, perh. fr. LL. bifax two- faced; L. bis + facies face. See Bi-, and cf. Face.

Be- and di- are often used interchangeably.

bib.etymology: From Bib, v., because the bib receives the drink that the child slavers from the mouth.

bible.etymology: F. bible, L. biblia, pl., fr. Gr. , pl. of , dim. of , , book, prop. Egyptian papyrus.

bibliographer.etymology: Gr. , fr. book + to write : cf. F. bibliographe.

bibliolatry.etymology: Gr. book + service, worship, to serve.

bibliomania.etymology: Gr. book + madness: cf. F. bibliomanie.

bibliophile.etymology: Gr. book + to love: cf. F. bibliophile.

bibliopole.etymology: L. bibliopola, Gr. ; book + to sell: cf. F. bibliopole.

bibulous.etymology: L. bibulus, fr. bibere to drink. See Bib, v. t.

bid.etymology: OE. bidden, prop to ask, beg, AS. biddan; akin to OS. biddian, Icel. bi, OHG. bittan, G. bitten, to pray, ask, request, and E. bead, also perh. to Gr. to persuade, L. fidere to trust, E. faith, and bide. But this word was early confused with OE. beden, beoden, AS. beódan, to offer, command; akin to Icel. bj, Goth. biudan (in comp.), OHG. biotan to command, bid, G. bieten, D. bieden, to offer, also to Gr. to learn by inquiry, Skr. budh to be awake, to heed, present OSlav. bud to be awake, E. bode, v. The word now has the form of OE. bidden to ask, but the meaning of OE. beden to command, except in "to bid beads." sq. root30.

bide.etymology: OE. biden, AS. bidan; akin to OHG. bitan, Goth. beidan, Icel. bi; perh. orig., to wait with trust, and akin to bid. See Bid, v. t., and cf. Abide.

bidet.etymology: F. bidet, perh. fr. Celtic; cr. Gael. bideach very little, diminutive, bidein a diminutive animal, W. bidan a weakly or sorry wretch.

bier.etymology: OE. bæe, beere, AS. b, b; akin to D. baar, OHG. bara, G. bahre, Icel barar, Dbaare, L. feretrum, Gr. , from the same bear to produce. See 1st Bear, and cf. Barrow.

biggin.etymology: F. béguin, prob. from the cap worn by the Béguines. Cf. Beguine, Biggon.

bight.etymology: OE. bi a bending; cf. Sw. & Dan. bugt bend, bay; fr. AS. byht, fr. b. sq. root88. Cf. Bout, Bought a bend, and see Bow, v.

It. s- bigottire to terrify, to appall. Wedgwood and others maintain that bigot is from the same source as Beguine, Beghard.

bismuth.etymology: Ger. bismuth, wismuth: cf. F. bismuth.

bison.etymology: L. bison, Gr. , a wild ox; akin to OHG. wisunt, wisant, G. wisent, AS. wesend, Icel. visundr: cf. F. bison.

bister.etymology: F. bistre a color made of soot; of unknown origin. Cf., however, LG. biester frowning, dark, ugly.

bite.etymology: OE. biten, AS. bitan; akin to D. bijten, OS. bitan, OHG. bizan, G. beissen, Goth. beitan, Icel. bita, Sw. bita, Dan. bide, L. findere to cleave, Skr. bhid to cleave. sq. root87. Cf. Fissure.

bittern.etymology: OE. bitoure, betore, bitter, fr. F. butor; of unknown origin.
